q: A passport is impounded 'in the public interest' with no reasons given and no hearing. The State argues that a statutory power was exercised and nothing more is required. Which statement best states the law?
options: The exercise fails: procedure depriving liberty must be fair, just and reasonable
The exercise stands: a power conferred by statute needs no further justification
The exercise fails: passports may not be impounded except during an Emergency
The exercise stands: reasons may be withheld where the public interest is invoked
expl: Existence of a statutory power is not enough; the procedure must independently be fair.
why: The second option states the overruled 1950 position, which is why it reads like orthodoxy. The fourth converts an invocation into a justification.
trapnote: A superseded doctrine offered as the current rule is the standard trap in this topic.

q: Consider: 1-A confession obtained by threat is inadmissible against the maker. 2-Narco-analysis without consent violates the protection against self-incrimination. 3-A specimen signature taken under compulsion violates it. Which is/are correct?
options: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: Coerced statements and involuntary narco-analysis are protected; a specimen signature is not.
why: All three concern compulsion, but only two concern testimony. The signature is material for comparison and falls outside.
trapnote: Group the three by what is being extracted: a statement, the contents of the mind, or a physical exemplar.

q: Dwellers are evicted at night with no notice. The State argues the guarantee of life protects mere physical existence. Which statement is correct?
options: The guarantee extends to shelter absolutely, and eviction is impermissible
The guarantee is confined to physical existence, and no procedure is required
The guarantee extends to dignity, and eviction requires a fair procedure
The guarantee applies only where the dwellers hold lawful title to the land
expl: Life means more than animal existence; deprivation requires a procedure that is fair.
why: The second option overstates the right into an absolute bar; the fourth makes the guarantee depend on title, which it does not.
trapnote: Expanded content does not mean an absolute right. Procedure remains the operative safeguard.

q: Arrest at 8 pm; grounds given next afternoon; production after forty hours excluding travel. Consider: 1-Grounds were defectively communicated. 2-The production rule was breached. 3-A later remand cures both. Correct?
options: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: Grounds must be communicated forthwith and production made within twenty-four hours; a later remand cures neither.
why: The third statement is the field misconception that a magistrate's order retrospectively legalises an illegal detention. It does not.
trapnote: A subsequent remand does not validate a detention that was illegal when it began.

q: A legislature enacts a vaguely worded prohibition on 'any criticism likely to cause disaffection', and officers enforce it broadly. Which statement is correct?
options: The provision is vulnerable: restrictions must be precise and the least invasive available
The provision is valid: vagueness affects enforcement alone and not the law itself
The provision is valid: disaffection is expressly a listed ground of restriction
The provision is vulnerable: restrictions on speech require a two-thirds majority
expl: Vagueness and overbreadth defeat reasonableness; disaffection is not a listed head.
why: The third option invents a listed ground that sounds historical and familiar, which is precisely why it is tempting.
trapnote: Check the listed heads before accepting any ground, however familiar its phrasing sounds.

q: Consider the role of a Magistrate at the stage of remand: 1-The Magistrate must satisfy himself that detention is necessary. 2-The case diary may be examined. 3-The Magistrate may grant remand mechanically where the police seek it. Which is/are correct?
options: 2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: Remand requires application of mind; mechanical orders defeat the safeguard.
why: The third statement describes common practice rather than law, which is what makes it attractive to a candidate reasoning from experience.
trapnote: Prevailing practice is not the legal standard. The safeguard exists precisely to prevent mechanical orders.

q: An officer asserts preventive detention may run indefinitely while the danger lasts. Which statement is correct?
options: Detention may continue indefinitely provided grounds are periodically reconsidered
Detention beyond three months requires the sanction of the State government alone
Beyond three months an Advisory Board opinion is needed unless Parliament otherwise provides
Detention may never exceed three months in the aggregate, in any case
expl: The three-month rule with its Board mechanism and its parliamentary exception governs.
why: The fourth option converts a procedural threshold into an absolute ceiling, which is the mirror image of the officer's error.
trapnote: Three months is a threshold triggering a safeguard, not an outer limit on detention.

q: A foreign national alleges custody torture and is told the protections are citizens-only. Consider: 1-Self-incrimination protection extends to him. 2-Life and personal liberty extend to him. 3-The six freedoms extend to him. Correct?
options: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: The penal and liberty protections reach every person; the six freedoms do not.
why: This tests the rights-holder distinction inside a single Part, where adjacent articles differ on precisely that point.
trapnote: Adjacent articles can differ on the rights-holder. Check each one rather than the Part as a whole.

q: Consider: 1-Assembly may be restricted in the interests of public order. 2-Association may be restricted in the interests of morality. 3-Movement may be restricted in the general public interest. Which is/are correct?
options: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: Each freedom carries its own restriction grounds, and all three statements pair correctly.
why: Set questions of this kind are usually built with one mismatched pair, so a set where all three match tests whether the candidate verifies rather than assumes.
trapnote: Do not assume a set must contain an error. Verify each pair against its own restriction clause.

q: A speech provokes a riot; arrests follow with no grounds given and no production; the arrested person's child is refused school. Which combination identifies the breaches?
options: A breach of the speech guarantee, and no breach of the arrest safeguards on these facts
Breaches of the speech guarantee and of the education right, the arrest being lawful
No breach on any limb, the riot justifying every step taken by the authorities
Speech restriction permissible, but arrest safeguards and the education right are breached
expl: Incitement is a listed ground, so the restriction stands; the arrest and education breaches remain.
why: Synthesis questions punish blanket answers. Each limb must be assessed on its own footing, and here they do not all fall the same way.
trapnote: In multi-limb scenarios, expect the limbs to resolve differently. A uniform answer is usually wrong.
